[![](data:image/png;base64,)](http://crossmark.crossref.org/dialog/?doi=10.1016/j.carbpol.2023.120619&domain=pdf)One-pot synthesis of magnetic cellulose nanocrystal and its post-functionalization for doxycycline adsorption

Ahmed I.A. Soliman [a,](#_bookmark0)b[, Jonathan A. Díaz Baca](#_bookmark1) [a, Pedram Fatehi a,](#_bookmark0)[\*](#_bookmark2)

a _Biorefining Research Institute and Chemical Engineering Department, Lakehead University, 955 Oliver Road, Thunder Bay, ON P7B5E1, Canada_

b _Chemistry Department, Faculty of Science, Assiut University, Assiut 71516, Egypt_

A R T I C L E I N F O

_Keywords:_

Cellulose nanocrystals Magnetic nanoparticles One-pot synthesis Doxycycline adsorption Carbohydrates

A B S T R A C T

The composite of magnetite (Fe3O4) and cellulose nanocrystal (CNC) is considered a potential adsorbent for water treatment and environmental remediation. In the current study, a one-pot hydrothermal procedure was utilized for magnetic cellulose nanocrystal (MCNC) development from microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) in the presence of ferric chloride, ferrous chloride, urea, and hydrochloric acid. The x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), x-ray diffraction (XRD), and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy analysis confirmed the presence of

CNC and Fe3O4, while transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and dynamic light scattering (DLS) analysis verified their respective sizes (< 400 nm and ≤ 20 nm) in the generated composite. To have an efficient adsorption activity for doxycycline hyclate (DOX), the produced MCNC was post-treated using chloroacetic acid

(CAA), chlorosulfonic acid (CSA), or iodobenzene (IB). The introduction of carboxylate, sulfonate, and phenyl groups in the post-treatment was confirmed by FTIR and XPS analysis. Such post treatments decreased the crystallinity index and thermal stability of the samples but improved their DOX adsorption capacity. The adsorption analysis at different pHs revealed the increase in the adsorption capacity by reducing the basicity of the medium due to decreasing electrostatic repulsions and inducing strong attractions.

# Introduction

Cellulose nanocrystal (CNC) is a non-toxic and renewable biode-gradable polymeric nanoparticle with a large surface area, and it can be used as an adsorbent, catalyst support, and flocculant ([Chen et al., 2018](#_bookmark24); [Das, Lindstro¨m, Sharma, Chi, & Hsiao, 2022](#_bookmark27)). In addition, CNC is considered a potential candidate for packing, coatings, electronics, ad-hesives, cosmetics, and drug delivery ([Chen et al., 2018](#_bookmark24); [Das et al., 2022](#_bookmark27); [Habibi, 2014](#_bookmark50); [Thomas et al., 2018](#_bookmark84)). Although there are reports about its functionality in these applications; chemical treatments, such as sulfo-nation, oxidation, esterification, etherification, silylation, amidation, or urethanization, were reported to improve its chemical and morpholog-ical structure, thermal stability, and adsorption performance ([Das et al.,](#_bookmark27) [2022](#_bookmark27); [Gericke, Trygg, & Fardim, 2013](#_bookmark40); [Habibi, 2014](#_bookmark50); [Ummartyotin &](#_bookmark86) [Manuspiya, 2015](#_bookmark86)).

The development of CNC has acquired a great interest, and different methods, e.g., acid hydrolysis ([Gunathilake, Ching, Uyama, Nguyen, &](#_bookmark44) [Chuah, 2021](#_bookmark44); Yunfeng [Guo, Zhang, Zheng, Li, & Yue, 2020](#_bookmark47)), oxidation ([Rahmatika et al., 2020](#_bookmark75); [Zhou et al., 2018](#_bookmark97)), and ionic liquid treatments ([Gericke et al., 2013](#_bookmark40); [Haron, Mahmood, Noh, Alam, & Moniruzzaman,](#_bookmark52)

[2021](#_bookmark52)) were applied to synthesize CNC from microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) and other bioresources. The acid hydrolysis using mineral acids, such as H2SO4, HCl, HNO3, or H3PO4, is a widely applied method for generating CNC ([Amin, Hosseinmardi, Martin, & Annamalai, 2022](#_bookmark18); [Camarero Espinosa, Kuhnt, Foster, & Weder, 2013](#_bookmark23); [Cheng et al., 2017](#_bookmark25); [Tang et al., 2021](#_bookmark83); [Zhao et al., 2022](#_bookmark96)). Alternatively, CNC can be gener-ated in the presence of inorganic halides, which function as a catalyst and facilitate the generation of CNC at a lower temperature ([Cheng](#_bookmark25) [et al., 2017](#_bookmark25); [Xi et al., 2022](#_bookmark94); [Zhao et al., 2022](#_bookmark96)).

Alternatively, CNC can be hybridized with metal oxide nano-materials to enhance its thermal stability, increase its surface area, and boost its catalytic activities ([Islam, Chen, Sisler, & Tam, 2018](#_bookmark57); [Oyewo,](#_bookmark72) [Elemike, Onwudiwe, & Onyango, 2020](#_bookmark72)). The presence of magnetite (Fe3O4) nanoparticles facilitates the efficient isolation of these hybrids from liquid media by applying an external magnetic field, and avoiding complicated separation processes, such as filtration or centrifugation ([Jabbar, Barzinjy, & Hamad, 2022](#_bookmark58); [Laurent et al., 2008](#_bookmark65); [Usman et al.,](#_bookmark87) [2018](#_bookmark87)). Among these hybrids, cellulose-based magnetite nanoparticles have found applications as catalysts, adsorbents, drug delivery pre-cursors, and sensors ([Gu et al., 2020](#_bookmark43); [He et al., 2021](#_bookmark53); [Katepetch &](#_bookmark61)

[Rujiravanit, 2011](#_bookmark61); [Kumar et al., 2022](#_bookmark64); [Yusefi et al., 2021](#_bookmark95); [Zirak,](#_bookmark98) [Abdollahiyan, Eftekhari-Sis, & Saraei, 2018](#_bookmark98)). Fe3O4 derived nano-particles can be synthesized through different methods, such as hydro-thermal, co-precipitation, and sol-gel ([Gawande, Branco, & Varma,](#_bookmark38) [2013](#_bookmark38); [Reddy, Arias, Nicolas, & Couvreur, 2012](#_bookmark76); [Usman et al., 2018](#_bookmark87)). Hydrothermal and co-precipitation methods are widely used to develop Fe3O4 and CNC composite ([Arantes et al., 2017](#_bookmark19); [Gu et al., 2020](#_bookmark43); J. [Guo](#_bookmark45) [et al., 2017](#_bookmark45); [Katepetch & Rujiravanit, 2011](#_bookmark61)). However, the development of Fe3O4@CNC, named magnetic CNC (MCNC), requires multiple steps, such as prior acid hydrolysis of cellulose into CNC, or prior Fe3O4 growth in the basic medium of ammonium hydroxide or sodium hydroxide, which is followed by the composite formation and is considered tire-some and complicated processes ([Haniffa et al., 2021](#_bookmark51)).

On the other hand, tetracyclines are widely used antibiotics,

considered toxic contaminants for microorganisms, plants, and animals ([Scaria, Anupama, & Nidheesh, 2021](#_bookmark79)). They are detected in soil and drinking water, and their removal through the biochemical and physi-cochemical processes from wastewater has been reported, where active adsorbents or catalysts were applied ([Gopal, Alex, Chandrasekaran, &](#_bookmark42) [Mukherjee, 2020](#_bookmark42); [Scaria et al., 2021](#_bookmark79)). Feizi et al. reported the adsorption of doxycycline hyclate (DOX), which is an analog of tetracyclines, on carboxyalkylated CNC, and the adsorption was strongly influenced by the carboxyalkylation process of CNC, as it activated the electrostatic attractions, π interactions, and hydrogen bonding with DOX ([Feizi &](#_bookmark30) [Fatehi, 2021b](#_bookmark30)). Also, sulfated CNC showed adsorption ability for the tetracycline hydrochloride due to the electrostatic attractions between the negatively charged sulfated CNC with the amine groups of tetracy-cline hydrochloride (J. [Liu et al., 2020](#_bookmark66)). Sun and coworkers investigated the tetracycline adsorption on magnetic cellulose, which was developed through the co-precipitation method ([Sun et al., 2021](#_bookmark81)). However, the influence of MCNC functionalization on the DOX adsorption capacity was not investigated to the best of our knowledge. In addition, the adsorption mechanism of DOX on MCNC has not been explored yet.

Taking advantage of the above findings and limitations of the pre-vious studies, one objective of this study is the creation of Fe3O4@CNC composite in a one-pot reaction vessel for the first time in this study, to the best of our knowledge, from MCC in the presence of FeCl3, FeCl2, urea, and hydrochloric acid. Another objective of this study is to activate the synthesized Fe3O4@CNC through post-treatment using chloroacetic acid (CAA), chlorosulfonic acid (CSA), or iodobenzene (IB) for DOX adsorption. The hydrodynamic size, zeta potential, crystallinity, morphology, chemical constituents, and thermal stability of the devel-oped and post-treated MCNC were investigated. The DOX adsorption was investigated using a quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation (QCM-D) and UV–Vis spectrophotometer. Factors affecting the DOX adsorption, such as the chemical modification method and pH values of the medium, were also investigated, which would be helpful in postu-lating the interactions between the adsorbents and DOX. Therefore, this study could be useful for a facile hydrothermal development of magnetic nanocellulose-based adsorbents for creating such adsorbents for haz-ardous material removals from wastewater.

# Experimental

- 1.  _Materials_

Ferric chloride hexahydrate (FeCl3.6H2O, 97 %), ferrous chloride tetrahydrate (FeCl2.4H2O, 98 %), microcrystalline cellulose (MCC, 51 μm), hydrochloric acid (37 %), urea (99 %), chlorosulfonic acid (CSA, 99 %), chloroacetic acid (CAA, 99 %), iodobenzene (IB,98 %), sodium hydroxide (97 %), dimethyl formamide (DMF), hydrogen peroxide (30

%, _w_/w), ammonium hydroxide (30 %, w/w), glycerol (99.5 %), iso-propanol (99.5 %), ethanol, and doxycycline hyclate (DOX, 93.5 %) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. The QCM-D sensors, gold-coated piezoelectric quartz crystal sensors, were purchased from Biolin Scien-tific Inc.

- 1.  _One-pot synthesis of MNCN_

In a Teflon-lined container (100 mL), 2 g of MCC, 1.6 g of FeCl3⋅6H2O, and 1.2 g of FeCl2⋅4H2O were vigorously stirred in 100 mL of HCl (4 M) for 20 min. Afterward, 25 g of urea was added to the Teflon container and stirred for 20 min. The Teflon container was sealed and transferred into a stainless-steel autoclave, which was heated at 120 ◦C, 150 ◦C, or 180 ◦C for 20 h. After cooling, the developed product, mag-netic cellulose nanocrystal (MCNC), was magnetically collected, washed three times using Milli-Q grade water, and dried at 60 ◦C.

- 1.  _Functionalization of the developed MNCN_

First, the MCNC was soaked in NaOH (0.01 M) for 2 h, and then collected and dried at 60 ◦C. For carboxymethylation, 0.5 g of NaOH-treated MCNC was dispersed in 100 mL of isopropanol at pH 12. The mixture was vigorously stirred for 0.5 h at 60 ◦C. Then, 1.25 g of CAA was added to the mixture and vigorously stirred (600 rpm) for 2 h. For sulfonation, 0.5 g of NaOH-treated MCNC and 240 μL of CSA were dispersed in 100 mL of DMF under gentle stirring (50 rpm) for 1 h at room temperature ([De Nino et al., 2020](#_bookmark28); [Gawande, Rathi, Nogueira,](#_bookmark39) [Varma, & Branco, 2013](#_bookmark39); [Luo, Semenikhin, Chang, Moon, & Kumar,](#_bookmark68) [2018](#_bookmark68); [Pingrey & Hsieh, 2022](#_bookmark73)). For phenylation, a 0.5 g of MCNC was dispersed in 100 mL DMF at a pH of 12 under vigorous stirring for 0.5 h at 80 ◦C followed by adding 0.5 mL of IB, and the reaction was continued for 2 h at 80 ◦C under vigorous stirring. After the reactions, the treated MCNC was magnetically collected from the reaction systems, washed in deionized water under sonication for three times, and dried at 60 ◦C.

- 1.  _Characterization_

Using a zeta analyzer (PALS, Nano Brook, Brookhaven, U.S.A.), the hydrodynamic diameter and zeta potential of MCNC derivatives were determined. In this experiment, 0.2 g of the MCNC samples were dispersed in 10 mL of deionized water. Before the measurements, the samples were kept under the vigorous stirring overnight and subse-quently sonicated for 3 min ([Feizi & Fatehi, 2021a, 2021b](#_bookmark29)). The hy-drodynamic diameter and zeta potential were calculated as the average of ten measurements.

Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy and x-ray photo-electron spectroscopy (XPS) were used to investigate the MNCN de-rivatives' chemical functional groups, surface elements and chemical bonds concentrations. The FTIR spectra were collected using Bruker Tensor 37, applying Attenuated total reflection (ATR) mode using a single-reflection ATR accessory equipped with a ZnSe crystal. The background spectrum from the environment and ATR crystal was collected prior to the sample measurement. Afterward, 0.01 g of the sample was placed on the ZnSe crystal and evenly pressed, and then the spectra were collected at a resolution of 4 cm—1 and 1024 scan cycles.

The X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (XPS) spectra were collected using a Kratos Axis Supra (Shimadzu Group Company, Japan) with a monochromatic Al Kα radiation at 15 kV with a pass energy of 20 eV. The obtained spectra were analyzed and deconvoluted using CasaXPS software.

The crystallinity of the samples was investigated by collecting the X-ray diffraction (XRD) spectra using Pananalytical X'pert Pro diffrac-tometer equipped with Cu Kα radiation at 1.5419 Å wavelength, 40 kV and 40 mA. The sample was placed onto a clean silicon substrate and submitted to the instrument, and the spectra were collected alongside the 2θ range of 6◦ and 70◦ with a resolution of 2◦/min. The background spectrum was collected from the Si substrate and subtracted from the sample's spectrum. The crystallinity index of cellulose (CI, %) was calculated using Eq. [(1)](#_bookmark3), where Icrystlline and Iamorphous were the in-tensities of peaks at the 2θ of 22.4◦ and 18.9◦, respectively.

Morphology, crystallinity, and elemental mapping of the samples were investigated using A ThermoFischer scientific Talos F200X Field emission scanning/transmission electron microscope (S/TEM) equipped with super-X four-quadrant energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS), where the excitation voltage of 200 kV was used.

Thermal gravimetric analysis (TGA, TGA i1000, Instrument Spe-cialists Inc.) was used to investigate the samples' thermal stability at a flow rate of 15 mL/min, which were heated from room temperature to 800 ◦C at the rate of 5 ◦C/min. The analysis was performed under a nitrogen atmosphere.

A force tensiometer (Attension Sigma 700/701, Biolin Scientific, Finland) equipped with a powder glass probe was used for estimating the water uptake by the samples according to the Washburn method ([Alwadani, Ghavidel, & Fatehi, 2021](#_bookmark16); [Feizi & Fatehi, 2021c](#_bookmark31)). Samples (1.0 g) were loaded into a cylindrical glass tube with an open base bottom, which was gradually immersed in a water bath, and the amount of absorbed water was estimated against the immersing time ([Alwadani](#_bookmark16) [et al., 2021](#_bookmark16); [Feizi & Fatehi, 2021c](#_bookmark31)). The measurements were repeated three times.

- 1.  _Adsorption analysis of DOX_
        1. _UV-VIS spectrophotometer_

The adsorption performance of doxycycline hyclate (DOX) on MCNC derivatives was studied using UV–vis Varian spectrophotometer. In this experiment, 0.1 g of samples was dispersed in 100 mL of DOX solution (20 mg/L) at pH 7. The experiment was continued for 3 h at 300 rpm shaking. At different time intervals, 5 mL sample was withdrawn, and the dispersed MCNC derivatives were magnetically removed for UV–Vis spectrum analysis. The adsorption efficiency and capacity of DOX on MCNC derivatives were calculated using Eqs. [(2) and (3)](#_bookmark4), respectively, where A0 and At are the adsorption values of DOX before adding the MCNC derivatives and at a certain t time. The qe, C0, Ce, V, and W are the adsorption capacity (mg/g), the initial concentration (mg/L), equilib-rium concentration (mg/L), the total volume of DOX (L), and the weight of adsorbent (g), respectively. The measurement was repeated three times.

# Results and discussion

- 1.  _MCNC production_
        1. _Crystalline structure of MCNC_

The XRD spectrum of MCC illustrated in [Fig. 1](#_bookmark5) shows diffraction peaks at 2θ of 14.9, 16.0, 20.4, 22.4, and 34.5◦, which are assigned to

planes (110), (110), (021), (200) and (004) of MCC, respectively ([Cheng](#_bookmark25) [et al., 2017](#_bookmark25); [Feizi & Fatehi, 2021a, 2021b](#_bookmark29)). The CI of MCC was calcu-lated to be 90.9 %. The co-precipitation method was utilized to develop Fe3O4 at room temperature as shown in the Supporting Information. The XRD spectrum of Fe3O4 shows diffraction peaks at 18.3◦, 30.1◦, 35.4◦, 37.1◦, 43.1◦, 53.5◦, 57.3◦, and 62.7◦, which are attributed to (111), (220), (311), (222), (400), (422), (511), and (440), respectively ([Gu](#_bookmark43)

[et al., 2020](#_bookmark43); [Rahmatika et al., 2020](#_bookmark75)). After the hydrothermal process at 180 ◦C, the XRD spectrum shows the diffraction patterns attributed to Fe3O4 and cellulose in the product of MCNC180. Fig. S1 shows the XRD spectra of the developed MCNC at 120 ◦C (for producing MCNC120) and 150 ◦C (for producing MCNC150), where the observed diffraction peaks were ascribed to cellulose, Fe3O4, and α-Fe2O3. The CI of cellulose in the MCNC120, MCNC150, and MCNC180 were 65.2 %, 71.4 %, and 84.4 %,

respectively. The decrease in the CI of cellulose in MCNC120 could be ascribed to the formation of cellulose carbamate, as the introduction of carbamate groups would disturb the hydrogen bonds between the cel-lulose chains ([Fu et al., 2015](#_bookmark32); [Gan et al., 2020](#_bookmark36)). The increase in the CI at 180 ◦C could be attributed to the hydrolysis of the carbamate groups under strongly basic conditions resulting in cellulose regeneration ([Fu](#_bookmark34) [et al., 2014](#_bookmark34); [Gan et al., 2017](#_bookmark35); [Hu, Li, Zhu, Zhang, & Zhu, 2021](#_bookmark55)).

The change in the XRD spectra shows that adjusting the hydrother-mal temperature is important for the development of Fe3O4. The basicity originated from the generated NH3 from the hydrothermal decomposi-

_2.5.2. Quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation (QCM-D)_

The adsorption of DOX on MCNC derivatives was comprehensively studied using a QCM-D instrument (Q-Sense Inc., Gothenborg, Sweden). Prior to the measurements, gold sensors were cleaned by exposing to UV/ozone (PSD Series, digital UV ozone system, NOVASCAN) for 15 min, immersing in a 60 ◦C preheated deionized water/hydrogen peroxide/ammonium hydroxide (5:1:1 _v_/v/v ratio) mixture for 5 min, rinsing with deionized water and ethanol, and again exposing to UV/ ozone for 15 min. After drying the cleaned sensors, the MCNC de-rivatives were spin-coated on them. The spin-coating was performed at 500 rpm for 1 min and 3000 rpm for 3 min using 20 μL of the MCNC solutions, which were prepared by dispersing 0.1 g of MCNC derivatives in 1 mL of deionized water and 10 μL of glycerol, which would facilitate the formation of a smooth layer and enhance its adhesion to the gold sensors ([Balzarotti, Cristiani, & Francis, 2017](#_bookmark21); [Valtakari et al., 2015](#_bookmark88)). The coated sensors were dried in an oven at 60 ◦C for 2 h before the measurement. Then, the sensors were placed onto the holder of the QCM-D instrument. Milli-Q grade water was used as a buffer solution for collecting the baseline by rinsing the substrate for 3 min, and the flow rate was fixed at 0.5 mL/min and 22 ± 2 ◦C. Afterward, the DOX (10 g/

- -   1.  _Chemical compositions of MCNC_

The FTIR spectrum of MCC is shown in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark6), where the absorption bands assigned to δ(O–H), and ʋ(O–H) vibrations were allocated at (660, and 1313 cm—1), and (3280 and 3332 cm—1), respectively ([De](#_bookmark28) [Nino et al., 2020](#_bookmark28); [Hu et al., 2021](#_bookmark55); [Luo et al., 2018](#_bookmark68)). Bands assigned to the δ(C–H), δ(CH2), and ʋ(CH2) vibrations were observed at 895, 1425, and 2895 cm—1, respectively ([De Nino et al., 2020](#_bookmark28); [Hu et al., 2021](#_bookmark55); [Luo et al.,](#_bookmark68) [2018](#_bookmark68)). Absorption band at 1615 was assigned to δ(O–H) of the adsor-bed water (X. [Guo, Liu, Wu, Fan, & Wu, 2018](#_bookmark46)). The FTIR spectra of MCNC120 and MCNC150 exhibited a new absorption band at 1712 cm—1 as illustrated in Fig. S2 in the Supplementary material, which was attributed to the ʋ(C=O) of the carbamate group ([Fu et al., 2014](#_bookmark33); Yi [Guo,](#_bookmark48) [Zhou, Wang, Zhang, & Lin, 2010](#_bookmark48); [Hu et al., 2021](#_bookmark55)). This band was not observed for MCNC180, which confirmed the hydrolysis of this group under severe conditions of high temperature (i.e., 180 ◦C) and strong basicity resulted in cellulose regeneration ([Fu, Yang, et al., 2014](#_bookmark33); [Gan,](#_bookmark37) [Zakaria, & Syed Jaafar, 2017](#_bookmark37); [Weißl et al., 2019](#_bookmark92)). These findings confirm that the CI increase in the cellulose of MCNC180 could be ascribed to the removal of carbamate groups and cellulose regeneration ([Fu, Yang,](#_bookmark33) [et al., 2014](#_bookmark33)).

The chemical groups of MCNC180 were also studied using XPS as shown in [Figs. 3](#_bookmark7) and S3, which would also clarify the influence of temperature on the developed magnetic cellulose. The C1s spectrum of MCC, illustrated in Fig. S3 in Supplementary material, was deconvoluted into three different components of C–C, C-O-H, and C-O-C at 285.0 eV,

286.6 eV, and 287.9 eV, respectively ([Jiao et al., 2018](#_bookmark59); [Sun et al., 2021](#_bookmark81)). The O1s spectrum (Fig. S3 in Supplementary material) represents both C-O-C and C-O-H components. Nitrogen or iron components were not detected in MCC as indicated from the N1s and Fe2p spectra illustrated in Fig. S3 in the Supplementary material. For MCNC120 and MCNC150, new peaks were observed under the C1s envelope at 288.4 eV and 289.5 eV (Fig. S3 in Supplementary materials), which could be ascribed to the

C–O of CONH2 and COO groups. The O1s spectra, Fig. S3 in Supple-

mentary material, showed three new deconvoluted peaks for MCNC120

and MCNC150, which were assigned to O–C (530.5 eV), Fe-O-Fe (531.8 eV), and Fe-O-H (533.7 eV) components and attributed to the presence of carbamate and iron oxides. The Fe2p spectra of MCNC120 and MCNC150, Fig. S3 in Supplementary materials, show two peaks at 712 eV and 726 eV, which were attributed to the Fe2p3/2 and Fe2p1/2, respectively. The presence of Fe–O, Fe2p3/2, and Fe2p1/2 confirms the formation of iron oxides, which is consistent with the XRD results (Fig. S1). The N1s spectrum showed the nitrogen components at 400.2

spectrum, [Fig. 3](#_bookmark7)a, completely disappeared, and the O–C peak at 530.5 eV in the O1s spectrum, [Fig. 3](#_bookmark7)b, decreased significantly, which indicates the complete hydrolysis of carbamate groups and cellulose regeneration and is in good agreement with the FTIR results ([Fig. 2](#_bookmark6)). Deconvolution of the N1s spec-trum, [Fig. 3](#_bookmark7)d, illustrates the presence of one peak representing the quaternary ammonium ions at 401.0 eV, and the absence of the NH2 assigned peak at 400.2 eV ([Wang et al., 2017](#_bookmark90)). The absence of the NH2 components is considered another evidence for the hydrolysis of carbamate groups at 180 ◦C. Wotton et al. reported that the hydro-thermal treatment of Fe2O3 at 180 ◦C in the presence of cellulose pro-duced Fe3O4 without requiring N2 purging or the presence of capping agents ([Wotton et al., 2021](#_bookmark93)). Based on the XRD, FTIR, and XPS results, the hydrothermal treatment of MCC at 120 ◦C or 150 ◦C in the presence of urea, FeCl3, and FeCl2 ions resulted in the synthesis of a composite containing cellulose carbamate, Fe3O4, and Fe2O3. With rising the temperature to 180 ◦C, the hydrothermal treatment was adequate for producing magnetic cellulose without the presence of α-Fe2O3, and cellulose carbamate.

- -   1.  _Size and morphology of MCNC_

The hydrodynamic diameters of MCNC120, MCNC150, and MCNC180 were determined to be >1672 nm, > 1100 nm, and 470 nm (± 60), respectively. In the absence of HCl, the MCC size decreased from 51,000 nm to >2200 nm. Cheng et al. reported that the hydrodynamic diameter of MCC decreased to 200–342 nm after the hydrothermal

treatment in the presence of different inorganic ([Cheng et al., 2017](#_bookmark25)). The drop in the MCC size to nanoscales illustrates that the applied hydro-thermal method at 180 ◦C (in the presence of Fe (III), Fe (II), urea, and HCl) was sufficient for converting the MCC to CNC and developing Fe3O4.

TEM and high resolution (HR)-TEM images of MCNC180 are

illustrated in [Figs. 4](#_bookmark8) and S4 (supporting information), where different particles with a nanoscale size (≤ 350 nm) were observed. The size of Fe3O4 nanoparticles was <20 nm. The dark field (DF)-TEM ([Fig. 4](#_bookmark8)e) and the corresponding EDX mapping ([Fig. 4](#_bookmark8)f) images show the distribution of Fe on the CNC domains, which confirms that the magnetically isolated

composite contains both cellulose and Fe3O4, and agrees with the XRD, FTIR, and XPS results. Based on these findings, the mechanistic routes for MCNC180 development were postulated in Fig. S5. The presence of HCl would acidify the medium (pH < 2), resulting in the hydrolysis of MCC to CNC in the presence of FeCl3 and FeCl2 ([Cheng et al., 2017](#_bookmark25); [Zhao](#_bookmark96)

[et al., 2022](#_bookmark96)). Urea reacts with cellulose producing cellulose carbamate, and the released ammonia neutralizes the HCl and reacts with Fe3+ and

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 4.** (a,b) TEM, (c,d) HR-TEM, (e) DF-TEM, and (f) Fe EDX-mapping images of MCNC180.

Fe2+ ions producing Fe3O4. Due to the medium basicity and high tem-perature (180 ◦C), the carbamate group was hydrolyzed, and cellulose was regenerated ([Fu, Zhou, et al., 2014](#_bookmark34); [Weißl et al., 2019](#_bookmark92)).

- 1.  _The post-treatment of MCNC180_
        1. _Crystalline structure of MCNC derivatives_

The MCNC180 modified by CAA, CSA, and IB to produce CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180, and IB-MCNC180, respectively. The crys-tallinity, chemical changes, thermal stability, and hydrodynamic diameter of post-treated MCNC180 were investigated. [Fig. 5](#_bookmark9) shows the XRD diffraction peaks of both crystalline cellulose and Fe3O4 in all post-treated MCNC180. The CI after reactions decreased to 75.4 %, 76.7 %, and 72.9 % for CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180, and IB-MCNC180,

respectively. The CI drop could be ascribed to the partial destruction of the cellulose crystallinity under strong chemical modifications ([Feizi](#_bookmark29) [& Fatehi, 2021a](#_bookmark29); [Luo et al., 2018](#_bookmark68)).

- -   1.  _Chemical compositions of MCNC derivatives_

The FTIR spectra of CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180, and IB-MCNC180 are shown in [Fig. 6](#_bookmark10). The spectrum of CAA-MCNC180 shows a new band at 1593 cm—1, and this band was attributed to the ʋ(COO—) confirming that the reaction between CAA and the CNC of MCNC180 in the presence of NaOH to produce sodium carboxymethylcellulose as illustrated in the plausible reaction (Fig. S6) ([Kamel, El-Gendy, Hassan,](#_bookmark60) [El-Sakhawy, & Kelnar, 2020](#_bookmark60); [Kono, Tsukamoto, & Tajima, 2021](#_bookmark62)). The FTIR spectrum of CSA-MCNC180 shows two new absorption bands at 810 cm—1 and 1235 cm—1, which were assigned to the ʋ(S=O) and ʋ (S–O), respectively ([De Nino et al., 2020](#_bookmark28); [Luo et al., 2018](#_bookmark68)). The pres-ence of these adsorption bands was attributed to the reaction of CSA and MCNC180 to produce sulfonic acid functionalized MCNC180 as illus-trated in Fig. S6. The spectrum of IB-MCNC180 shows an absorption band at 3017 cm—1, 1413 cm—1, and 742 cm—1, which is assigned to the ʋ (C–H) aromatic, ʋ(C=C), and Out-of-plane aromatic δ(C–H) vibrations of aromatics ([Silverstein, Webster, Kiemle, & Bryce, 2014](#_bookmark80)). The presence of these absorption bands confirms the presence of aromatic components after the post-treatment.

Also, XPS was used for determining the chemical structures of MCNC180 after post-treatment. The XPS C1s spectrum ([Fig. 7](#_bookmark11)a) of CAA-MCNC180 was deconvoluted into 4 peaks, which were assigned to C–C, C-O-H, C-O-C, and COO components. The abundance of the C–C com-ponents increased compared to that of MCNC180 ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark7)a), which is attributed to the grafting of CAA. The deconvoluted peak at 289.4 eV is attributed to the COO components, which is in good agreement with the

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 5.** XRD spectra of CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180, and IB-MCNC180.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 6.** ATR-FTIR spectra of CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180, and IB-MCNC180.

FTIR spectrum ([Fig. 6](#_bookmark10)). These COO components were also observed in the O1s spectrum ([Fig. 7](#_bookmark11)b) at 530.2 eV, which is attributed to the O–C components. The components of Fe–O and O–H were also observed

under the O1s envelope ([Fig. 7](#_bookmark11)b). The Fe components were also observed from the XPS Fe2p spectrum ([Fig. 7](#_bookmark11)c), which was also illus-trated from the XRD spectrum of CAA-MCNC180, ([Fig. 6](#_bookmark10)), where the diffraction patterns of Fe3O4 components were observed. After CSA post-treatment, the peak assigned to the C-O-SO3H was observed at 289.7 eV under the C1s envelope, and the peaks attributed to C–C, C-O-H, and C-O-C components were also observed. The presence of sulfur is confirmed from the XPS S2p spectrum as shown in Fig. S7, where two peaks assigned to S2p3/2 and S2p1/2 of the sulfonic group were observed at

168.5 eV and 169.7 eV, respectively ([Choudhary et al., 2021](#_bookmark26)). The

change in the O1s spectrum of CSA-MCNC180 is attributed to the presence of S–O, and S-O-H components besides C–O and Fe–O

components. Despite the strong acidic properties of the CSA, the above-mentioned post-treatment procedures were applicable of functionalizing MCNC180 without removing Fe3O4 as indicated by the presence of Fe2p3/2 and Fe2p1/2 peaks (XPS Fe2p spectrum in [Fig. 7](#_bookmark11)c) and from the XRD spectrum ([Fig. 5](#_bookmark9)). The XPS C1s spectrum of IB-MCNC180 was

deconvoluted in [Fig. 7](#_bookmark11)a, and the peak at 284.6 eV was ascribed to the C–C of phenyl components. [Fig. 7](#_bookmark11)b shows a clear change in the XPS O1s spectrum, which shows three apexes attributing to O-C=C, Fe–O, and C–O as observed at 529.9 eV, 531.2 eV, and 532.8 eV, respectively. The

XPS Fe2p spectrum of IB-MCNC180 shows the two peaks of Fe2p3/2 and Fe2p1/2. These XPS results support the successful post-treatment of MCNC180 using the CAA, CSA, and IB.

- -   1.  _Size and morphology of MCNC derivatives_

The hydrodynamic diameter of CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180, and IB-MCNC180 were 469 (± 23) nm, 391 (± 25) nm, and 500 (± 43) nm,

respectively. These apparent sizes indicated that the modified MCNC180s were still at the nanoscale without a significant formation of microscale aggregations.

The TEM images of CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180, and IB-

MCNC180 are illustrated in [Figs. 8](#_bookmark12) and S8, where hexagonal, and cubic-like Fe3O4 were observed on CNC. The CNC nanoparticles kept their nanoscale without large aggregations. The spacing fringes of (311) and (200) planes of Fe3O4 nanoparticles were 0.26 nm and 0.31 nm, respectively ([Usman et al., 2018](#_bookmark87)). Fig. S9 shows the HR-TEM and EDX mapping of carbon, sulfur, and iron distributed on the CSA-MCNC180,

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)**Fig. 7.** XPS (a) deconvoluted C1s, (b) O1s, and (c) Fe2p spectra of CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180 and IB-MCNC180.

which illustrated that the distribution of SO3H was distributed on the Fe3O4 and CNC particles ([De Nino et al., 2020](#_bookmark28); [Gawande, Branco, &](#_bookmark38) [Varma, 2013](#_bookmark38); [Gawande, Rathi, et al., 2013](#_bookmark39); [Luo et al., 2018](#_bookmark68)).

- -   1.  _Thermal stability of MCNC derivatives_

The change in the chemical structure would generally yield an alteration in the thermal stability of materials. The TGA and DTA curves of the MCNC180, CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180, and IB-MCNC180 are

illustrated in [Fig. 9](#_bookmark13). The TGA curve of MCNC180 ([Fig. 9](#_bookmark13)a) showed a weight loss of <5 % in the range of 0–310 ◦C, which is attributed to the adsorbed moisture ([Liu, Guo, Nan, Duan, & Zhang, 2017](#_bookmark67); [Merlini et al.,](#_bookmark69) [2020](#_bookmark69); [Nan et al., 2017](#_bookmark70)). The weight loss in the range of 310–500 ◦C

could be attributed to the cellulose degradation and Fe3O4 trans-formation to Fe2O3 ([Bahadur et al., 2017](#_bookmark20);[Liu et al., 2017](#_bookmark67) ; [Merlini et al.,](#_bookmark69) [2020](#_bookmark69) ; [Nan et al., 2017](#_bookmark70)). The degradation of cellulose occurred through

**Fig. 8.** TEM and HR-TEM images of (a,b) CAA-MCNC180, (c,d) CSA-MCNC180,

and (e,f) IB-MCNC180, respectively.

depolymerization, dehydration, and decomposition of glycosidic units, and formation of charred residues ([Liu et al., 2017](#_bookmark67); [Merlini et al., 2020](#_bookmark69); [Nan et al., 2017](#_bookmark70)). The weight loss in the range of 310–500 ◦C occurred in two steps of 310–360 ◦C (26 %) and 360–500 ◦C (25 %). In the DTA curve ([Fig. 9](#_bookmark13)b), two peaks were observed at 335 ◦C and 440 ◦C, which were attributed to the cellulose degradation process. Peaks at <100 ◦C

and 482 ◦C were attributed to the moisture desorption and trans-

formation of Fe3O4 to Fe2O3 ([Bahadur et al., 2017](#_bookmark20)). The thermograph of CAA-MCNC180 shows the mass loss in two stages at <100 ◦C and 280–585 ◦C, which were attributed to the moisture desorption, cellulose

degradation, and Fe3O4 phase transformation to Fe2O3. The degradation of cellulose in the CAA-MCNC180 started at a lower temperature than that of MCNC180, indicating the decrease in the cellulose thermal sta-bility due to the crystallinity decrease as indicated by the XRD results ([Wei et al., 2019](#_bookmark91)). The DTA curve of CAA-MCNC180 shows the main peak at 330 ◦C, which could be ascribed to cellulose degradation. The TGA and DTA curves of CSA-MCNC180 show a significant decrease in thermal stability, and the degradation started at 185 ◦C due to the removal of sulfonic groups. Also, the degradation was completed at

455 ◦C, indicating the decrease in the thermal stability due to the

crystallinity decrease and the introduction of sulfonate groups ([Camar-ero Espinosa et al., 2013](#_bookmark23); Yunfeng [Guo et al., 2020](#_bookmark47); [Zoppe, Johansson, &](#_bookmark99) [Sepp¨ala¨, 2015](#_bookmark99)). The TGA and DTA results of IB-MCNC180 show a slight decrease in the thermal stability, and the primary degradation occur-rence at 300–520 ◦C.

![Image of Fig. 9](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 9.** (a) TGA and (b) DTA curves of MCNC180, CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180, and IB-MCNC180 samples.

- -   1.  _Water uptake of MCNC derivatives_

The water uptake of the samples was investigated, and the results are presented in Fig. S10. The values calculated from the Washburn method were 3.9 (± 0.43), 2.7 (± 0.20), 3.4 (± 0.15), 3.1 (± 0.20), and 2.6 (± 0.38) g/g of MCC, MCNC180, CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180, and IB-

MCNC180, respectively. The lower water uptake of the MCNC180 before and after post-treatment than MCC was attributed to the presence of CNC, grafting of Fe3O4, and the presence of hydrophobic moieties, which would reduce the free hydroxyl groups exposed to the water preventing the water penetration ([Popescu, Dogaru, & Popescu, 2017](#_bookmark74)). It has been reported that adding CNC to a polymeric matrix would reduce the water uptake owing to the occurrence of physical bonding between the polymer matrix and CNC' surface hydroxy groups ([Popescu](#_bookmark74) [et al., 2017](#_bookmark74)). The water uptake of CAA-MCNC180 and CSA-MCNC180 was more than that of MCNC180 due to the presence of hydrophilic carboxyl and sulfonic groups, respectively. Also, the water uptake of IB-MCNC180 was slightly lower than that of MCNC180 due to the intro-duction of hydrophobic phenyl groups.

- 1.  _DOX adsorption_
        1. _UV-VIS spectrophotometer analysis_

The DOX adsorption efficiency and the adsorbed quantities of DOX on MCNC180, CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180, and IB-MCNC180

measured via the UV–Vis analysis (Eqs. [(2) and (3)](#_bookmark4)) are illustrated in [Fig. 10](#_bookmark14). The absorbance at the λmax of 346 nm shown in Fig. S11 was used to calculate the removal efficiency of DOX. Generally, the adsorption efficiency and the adsorbed quantities were higher after post-treatment on the MCNC180. The presence of carboxylate, sulfonic, and phenyl groups in CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180, and IB-MCNC180 would enhance the DOX adsorption, respectively, as these groups would facilitate the hydrogen bonding, electrostatic interactions, and π-π stacking with DOX ([Feizi & Fatehi, 2021b](#_bookmark30); [Olusegun & Mohallem,](#_bookmark71) [2020](#_bookmark71); [Rodrigues Filho et al., 2011](#_bookmark77)).

- -   1.  _QCM-D analysis_

[Fig. 11](#_bookmark15)a shows the frequency (ΔF) and dissipation (ΔD) of the sen-sors coated with MCNC180, CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180, or IB-MCNC180 as a function of time during the DOX adsorption. The MCNC180 showed a slight decrease in the ΔF shifts, while CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180, and IB-MCNC180 exhibited significant re-ductions in the ΔF shifts. Also, the ΔD increased as time elapsed for all samples. These results indicate the adsorption of DOX on the sensors. As previously stated, the presence of carboxylate and sulfonate groups on CAA-MCNC180 and CSA-MCNC180 would enhance the electrostatic interactions of these groups with the amino and amide groups of DOX,

respectively. In the case of IB-MCNC180, the presence of phenyl group results in the π-π stacking with the DOX aromatic and C–O moieties.

[Fig. 11](#_bookmark15)b shows the changes in the adsorbed mass of DOX on MCNC180, CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180, and IB-MCNC180 as a

function of time at pH 7. As seen, the adsorbed DOX was 4.2 mg/m2 for MCNC180, while it was 52.1 (± 6), 61.2 (± 7), and 32.3 (± 5) mg/m2 for CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180, and IB-MCNC180, respectively. The increase in the adsorbed mass of DOX on CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180, and IB-MCNC180 illustrates the significance of the post-treatment for DOX adsorption. Plotting ΔD versus ΔF of the adsorbed DOX on the samples at pH 7 ([Fig. 11](#_bookmark15)c) would demonstrate the correla-tion of the viscoelasticity and mass ratio of the adsorbed DOX ([Feizi &](#_bookmark29) [Fatehi, 2021a, 2021b](#_bookmark29); [Kou & Xu, 2016](#_bookmark63)). The steeper slope demonstrates that the absorbed DOX layer was viscoelastic and expanded.

In contrast, a lower slope describes a compact and relatively rigid layer ([Feizi & Fatehi, 2021a, 2021b](#_bookmark29); [Huellemeier, Eren, Ortega-Anaya,](#_bookmark56) [Jimenez-Flores, & Heldman, 2022](#_bookmark56); [Kou & Xu, 2016](#_bookmark63)). As illustrated, the ΔD/ΔF slope of CSA-MCNC180 shows two stages of a compact and rigid DOX layer defined from a lower slope, which could be attributed to the electrostatic attractions between the SO3H of CSA-MCNC180 and

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 10.** The DOX (a) adsorption efficiency (%) and (b) qe (mg/g) versus time (min).

NH2 groups of DOX ([Feizi & Fatehi, 2021b](#_bookmark30)). The second stage, where the steeper slope was observed, indicates that the adsorbed layer was less dense. Due to the increase in water uptake (Fig. S10) and extra DOX adsorption, the rigidity of the adsorbed DOX layers decreased, and they became viscoelastic ([Benedetti & Torresi, 2013](#_bookmark22); [Hopa & Fatehi, 2020](#_bookmark54)). In the case of IB-MCNC180, the lower slope of the ΔD/ΔF plot indicates that the adsorbed DOX developed a more rigid DOX layer; and the low water uptake (Fig. S10), low adsorbed mass, and strong π-π stacking could be the reasons for the rigidness of the DOX adsorbed layer.

As reported, the net charge of DOX at pH < 2.5, pH = 4–7, and pH >

8 equals +1, 0, and —1, respectively ([Savadi, Lotfipour, McMillan,](#_bookmark78)

[Hashemzadeh, & Hallaj-Nezhadi, 2022](#_bookmark78)). The alteration in the charac-teristics (i.e., surface potential, hydrodynamic diameters, water uptake, and the chemical natures) of the MCNC before and after post function-alization could depict how the alteration in the physicochemical prop-erties of MCNC would impact the DOX adsorption. The effect of pH of the medium on the adsorbed DOX on MCNC180 derivatives is illustrated in [Figs. 11](#_bookmark15)d and S12. The adsorbed DOX amounts on CSA-MCNC180 at

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 11.** The DOX adsorption of MCNC180, CAA-MCNC180, CSA-MCNC180,

and IB-MCNC180 using QCM-D at pH 7, (a) changes in frequencies versus time (_sec_), (b) changes in dissipations versus frequencies (ΔF / Hz), (c) adsorbed mass versus time (sec), and (d) changes in the maximum adsorbed mass (mg/ m2) at different pH values calculated by QCM.

different pH values of the medium can be ordered as MpH 3 > MpH 7 > MpH 10. The value of zeta potential (ζ) of CSA-MCNC180 at pH 3 (Fig. S13) confirms the strong acidic properties, which results in higher

DOX adsorption due to the strong electrostatic attraction between SO3H (i.e., acidic group) and the DOX amine and amide groups (i.e., basic groups) as schematically illustrated in Fig. S14. The electrostatic re-pulsions increase with increasing the pH resulting in the suppression of overall DOX adsorption on CSA-MCNC180 at pH 10 (Fig. S14) ([Feizi &](#_bookmark30) [Fatehi, 2021b](#_bookmark30)). The adsorbed DOX was higher on CAA-MCNC180 at pH 7 than at pH 3, as the presence of deprotonated carboxylate anions at pH 7 might promote the hydrogen bonding and π-π interactions between CAA-MCNC180 and DOX, which is in agreement with the higher DOX adsorption on carboxypantadecanated CNC at pH 7 reported by [Feizi](#_bookmark30) [and Fatehi (2021b)](#_bookmark30). In the case of IB-MCNC180, the DOX adsorption occurred at pH 3 and pH 7 was due to the π-π stacking, and the increase in the electrostatic attractions would reduce the DOX adsorption. At pH

3 and 7, the insignificant DOX adsorption on MCNC180 could be ascribed to the competition between the hydronium ions and cationic moieties of DOX, which could induce the electrostatic repulsions with the DOX molecules ([Amaly, El-Moghazy, Nitin, Sun, & Pandey, 2022](#_bookmark17); [Tan, Sabar, & Hussin, 2018](#_bookmark82)). While the increase of DOX adsorption at pH 10 could induce the hydrogen bonding between of MCNC180 and anionic moieties of DOX ([Amaly et al., 2022](#_bookmark17); [Tan et al., 2018](#_bookmark82)). A com-parison of the DOX adsorption illustrated in [Fig. 11](#_bookmark15)d reveals that the sulfonation would make the MCNC180 more active towards DOX adsorption than the carboxymethylation and phenylation post-treatment. Comparing the results presented in [Figs. 11](#_bookmark15)d, S15 and S16 indicates that the post-rinsing of the MCNC adsorbents with water after DOX adsorption could be a strategy for recovering the majority of the

adsorbed DOX amounts (>55 %) and for cleaning the adsorbents for

their use in the next cycle. Although the post-rinsing was not sufficient to recover all the adsorbed DOX, it could be considered a steppingstone to develop a desorption pathway for the desorption of DOX from the adsorbent. However, process optimization is necessary to achieve the

maximum DOX recovery from the MCNC, which will be considered in future research.

Table S1 in the supplementary material lists the adsorption capac-ities of MCNC, CAA-MCNC, CSA-MCNC and IB-MCNC for DOX, and it compares the adsorption results of MCNC derivatives with those avail-able in the literature. Evidently, post functionalized MCNC had com-parable adsorption capacities with the reported adsorbents, which make them promising adsorbents.

# Conclusions

In this research, the composite of CNC and Fe3O4 nanoparticles was successfully developed from MCC through a one-pot hydrothermal process at 180 ◦C in the presence of FeCl3, FeCl2, urea, and HCl. The lower reaction temperatures were not desirable for MCNC development due to the presence of Fe2O3 and cellulose carbamate with a size >1100 nm. Due to the insignificant adsorption capacity of the developed

MCNC180 towards DOX drugs, it was subjected to carboxylation, sul-fonation, or phenylation. The post-functionalization of MCNC180 led to the preservation of morphological and crystalline structures with decreasing the CI of cellulose components, a decrease in thermal sta-bility, and a change in water uptake of the sample. The post-treatment altered the DOX adsorption capacity by elevating the interactions be-tween DOX and MCNC derivatives via hydrogen bonding, electrostatic attractions, and π-π stacking. The adsorption capacity was influenced significantly by the pH of the medium. The highest DOX adsorption capacity was for CSA-MCNC180 in the acidic medium due to the pres-ence of strong SO3H acidic groups, which would be electrostatically attracted to amino and amide groups of DOX. Increasing the basicity of the medium resulted in a decrease in the DOX adsorption due to the occurrence of electrostatic repulsions. This study shows a considerable advantage in the engineering and functionalization of a sustainable magnetic CNC through one-pot hydrothermal procedures followed by post-treatment for enhancing the drug, such as DOX, removal from wastewater.
